title: Title
notes: Open by positioning the appendix as a service room for the whole course. The symbols are not ornamental special functions; each one performs a statistical job on a curved sample space, such as normalizing a density, predicting a resultant length, or turning a moment equation into an estimate.

title: Route
notes: Use the route slide to prevent the appendix from becoming a list of unrelated formulas. The organizing habit is to attach every function to a job: Bessel ratios estimate concentration, normalizers make densities legal, Kummer ratios compute axial moments, and integral checks keep the geometry visible.

title: Function Map
notes: Draw attention to the map rather than the names. The circular case begins with modified Bessel functions of low order, spherical models shift the order with dimension, axial models call on Kummer functions, and frame models generalize the same averaging idea over a larger curved space.

title: Bessel Normalizer
notes: Connect the formula to mass on the sphere. The Bessel function is not an arbitrary constant; it is what remains after the exponential tilt has been integrated around every direction. The visual cap also previews why large concentration creates numerical overflow and quadrature sensitivity.

title: Bessel Ratio Atlas
notes: Use this slide as the main mental model for concentration estimation. The ratio is monotone, so inversion is well posed, but the same kappa does not mean the same visible clustering across dimensions. Students should inspect the ordering of the curves before touching a root finder.

title: Inverting Concentration
notes: Frame concentration estimation as a numerical inverse problem with a visible domain. The observed resultant length must lie between zero and one, the monotonic curve gives a unique solution, and the residual after substituting the estimate back into A_p is the simplest reliability certificate.

title: Approximation Regimes
notes: Make the approximation message practical rather than formal. The appendix gives local formulas, but the notebook turns them into error plots. In the middle regime students should prefer exact evaluation or numerical inversion, because neither the low concentration nor the high concentration story is yet trustworthy.

title: Stable Normalizer Arithmetic
notes: Spend a minute on computation because this appendix is used by later fitting routines. The safe implementation often works with logarithms, scaled special functions, or direct ratios. Otherwise the code can fail in high concentration exactly where the statistical signal is strongest.

title: Kummer Axial Moments
notes: Contrast the Kummer derivative ratio with A_p. A directional first moment vanishes under uniformity, but an axial squared projection has baseline one over p. That single distinction explains why the Kummer curve begins above zero and why axial models use second moment language.

title: Kummer Identity Check
notes: Use this slide to connect symbolic identities to numerical trust. The derivative formula supplies an analytic ratio, while a finite difference of log M gives an independent check. When those curves agree, the learner sees the moment calculation and the implementation test at the same time.

title: Stiefel Integral
notes: Make the Stiefel language less intimidating by starting with one frame. In three dimensions that object is just a unit vector on the sphere. Averaging exp(kappa X_1) over a deterministic sphere grid gives a direct check against sinh kappa over kappa.

title: Normalizers As Averages
notes: This slide turns normalizing constants into measurable objects. Learners should see two routes to the same number: a special-function formula and a deterministic average over the relevant curved space. Agreement between them is evidence that the implementation respects the geometry.

title: Table Replacement Lab
notes: Describe the table replacement as a reproducibility pattern. The estimate alone is not enough; the notebook also stores the input statistic and the residual after the equation is solved. That residual is what lets later chapters trust a computed concentration instead of consulting a fixed row.

title: Notebook Artifacts
notes: Connect the deck back to the notebook without turning the slide into a file inventory. The key evidence is invariant based: monotonicity, inverse round trips, derivative agreement, and integral agreement. Those checks make the special-function appendix usable by later modeling chapters.

title: Recap
notes: Close with a routing question that students can use in later chapters. Before evaluating any special function, identify whether the model needs a first moment, an axial second moment, or a normalizing average. That choice determines the calculator and the sanity check.
